The most widespread is the khlui phīang aw; the traditional B-flat version mostly accompanies Thai songs and Thai ensembles, while the later C version was adjusted to suit the Western chromatic scale. Because its range is higher and its timbre brighter, the khlui lip often appears alongside the khlui phīang aw in bands and ensembles and is regarded as a leading instrument, like the ranat ek and the saw duang. The khlui ū is also used in many Thai bands and ensembles.

It is used in Thai traditional songs, ensembles and bands, and for informal playing; the commonest, the khlui phīang aw, has a middle range, and there are a smaller khlui lip and a larger khlui ū.

克魯伊笛為垂直吹奏的氣鳴樂器。演奏時以垂直方式持笛，左手拇指負責按背面的指孔，其: The khlui is an aerophone blown vertically. Hold the flute upright; the left thumb takes the hole on the back and the remaining fingers the seven holes on the front. There is a wooden plug at the mouthpiece and a square window at the side, where the sound is produced; opening and closing the holes changes the pitch. A beginner should first learn where the eight holes are and how to finger them, then keep the blowing steady.
克魯伊笛為泰國豎吹氣鳴笛，起源於素可泰時期之前或期間（1238–1583）。14: The khlui is a Thai end-blown aerophone, originating before or during the Sukhothai period (1238–1583). King Trailokkanat, who reigned from 1431 to 1488, set official models for traditional Thai instruments, giving it formal recognition. After generations of modification, three main forms survive — khlui phīang aw, khlui lip and khlui ū — with several variants; it resembles the Cambodian khloy. The khlui lip was later developed to play with the khlui phīang aw in band ensembles, and the C khlui was modified to suit the Western chromatic scale. Because tropical hardwoods are scarce, plastic is also used for more ordinary instruments.
克魯伊笛為豎吹氣鳴樂器，靠吹口木塞與方形孔發聲；指孔多等距排列，約將八度分為七個: The khlui is an end-blown aerophone, sounding through the wooden plug and square window at the mouthpiece; the fingerholes are mostly evenly spaced, dividing the octave into seven roughly equal steps. The middle-sized khlui has a moderate range, an octave above middle C, and the traditional B-flat instrument is a little below Western standard pitch. The small khlui has the highest range and the most prominent timbre, the large khlui the lowest. The source does not record how its volume is controlled.
